I have worked as a conference interpreter for almost twenty years, and people often think my job is to translate words. It isn't. My job is to carry meaning from one language to another, and those are very different things. When a speaker says something that could mean two things, I can't stop the meeting and ask. So I listen for the intention behind the words, and I choose the version that the speaker would recognize as their own. In my private work, with lawyers and business people, I can ask, and I always do. I say: so what you're saying is this, or, if I've understood correctly, you mean that. Some clients find it slow at first. Then, one day, that one question saves them from an expensive mistake, and they never complain again. The most dangerous moment in any negotiation is when both sides nod. Nodding feels like agreement, but very often it only means that each person heard what they expected to hear.

For twelve years I was a police negotiator. Now I teach negotiation to executives, and the first thing I teach them is the skill that saved the most lives in my old job: paraphrasing. When people are under pressure, they don't need you to agree with them. They need to know that you have understood them. So you take what they said and give it back in your own words, shorter and calmer. You don't add your opinion, and you don't correct them yet. If you get it wrong, that's fine: they will correct you, and now you have better information. Executives always want to skip this step and go straight to the solution. I ask them to try it in one meeting a week. The results surprise them. The other side talks more, gives away more, and is much more likely to say yes at the end, because a person who feels understood is a person who feels safe.
